I am 46 years old and have farmed these lands in Quzhou County since I was a young girl. My family has about 7 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. Around here, there is only one sensible way to use this soil and climate: the winter wheat–summer maize double crop that everyone in our village grows. The wheat I sowed last October is already at jointing stage. I will top-dress it with urea now and irrigate three more times before early June harvest — at booting, heading, and grain-filling if the rains stay away. I will also spray fungicide twice to prevent rust and powdery mildew, which always trouble our humid springs, and watch for aphids. After the combine takes the wheat off in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid maize — likely Nongda 372 or another variety from the village supply store — using no-tillage direct seeding, which saves fuel and precious days during the busy summer turnaround. I will put compound fertilizer in the seed furrow at sowing and side-dress nitrogen when the maize reaches knee height. I will irrigate twice, at jointing and at silking. I am not going to experiment with vegetables or cotton this year; grain prices are stable, I know this rotation well, and my husband works part-time in Handan, so most of the fieldwork falls on me. I cannot afford a crop I do not fully understand.
